title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest spans your five tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Findings are drawn from recent, reputable sources (PubMed/PMC, JAMA/Nature, NIH ClinicalTrials.gov, Frontiers, Springer, and clinical-practice guidelines), with citations linked as chips under each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.body:
This week reinforces a familiar pattern: **topicals have the strongest proof, supplements are a mixed bag, and "longevity drugs" stay experimental.**

- **Urolithin A keeps gaining human data.** A 2025 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in *Nature Aging* (50 healthy middle-aged adults, **1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks**) found UA shifted immune cells toward **younger, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells** and improved mitochondrial and immune function — early but encouraging evidence against "inflammaging." A **2026 iScience** study showed a **topical** UA formulation activates skin-cell mitophagy and improves mitochondrial function. An **NIH/NIA trial (NCT06274749)** testing UA on glucose metabolism in adults 55+ is set to begin recruiting **Nov 26, 2026**.
- **NAD+ boosters: biomarkers up, benefits unclear.** A 2026 *npj Aging* RCT gave adults ≥65 **high-dose NMN (1,250 mg/day) for 24 weeks**. It robustly raised blood NAD+ but showed **no significant improvement** in hearing or physical performance — a reminder that moving a biomarker isn't the same as moving health.
- **Rapamycin stays experimental.** A 2026 review concludes there is still **no clear clinical evidence** that rapamycin/rapalogs safely slow aging in healthy humans; even the larger PEARL trial showed only modest, exploratory secondary effects (e.g., muscle mass and self-reported pain in women). Treat as investigational, not a regimen.
- **For skin, retinoids remain the gold standard.** A 2025 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (1,361 patients) confirms **topical tretinoin** significantly improves fine and coarse photoaging wrinkles. **At-home red/near-infrared LED devices** (2026 systematic review, 8 studies, 365 people) show modest gains in wrinkles, texture, and elasticity — but trials are small and often industry-funded, so keep expectations measured.

Practical framing: prioritize interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and be skeptical of single-ingredient "reverse aging" marketing.

sections.body:
New 2026 meta-analyses keep the same headline: **HIIT is a time-efficient way to drive cardio fitness — but pair it with strength work for a complete program.**

- **Middle-aged & older women.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* review (19 RCTs) found HIIT **significantly improves VO2max** (SMD 1.20, *high* certainty) but did **not** reliably improve muscle strength, flexibility, or sit-to-stand performance. Translation: HIIT alone isn't enough for functional fitness — **add resistance training.**
- **Women with overweight/obesity.** A separate 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* meta-analysis (15 RCTs) found HIIT reduced **body weight, BMI, body-fat %, and fat mass**, raised VO2max, and nudged **HDL up / LDL down** — favoring body recomposition over big scale drops.
- **PCOS.** A network meta-analysis (23 RCTs, ~1,192 women) ranked **HIIT best** for VO2max, fasting insulin, and LDL, while **moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT)** ranked best for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). A blended week can capture both.
- **Heart health.** A 2026 RCT in women with obesity found **only HIIT** (not MICT) improved **myocardial work efficiency** on echocardiography — a hint of cardiac benefit beyond fitness scores.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and metabolic wins; **add strength training**, progress volume gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's trials sharpen *how* to do it well.

- **PFMT beats Pilates — clearly.** A 3-arm RCT (*International Urogynecology Journal*, Oct 2026; 105 women) compared PFMT, Pilates, and Pilates + voluntary pelvic-floor contraction. PFMT produced a far larger drop in incontinence impact (**ICIQ-SF −4.4 vs −0.7**) and much bigger gains in muscle strength and squeeze pressure. Targeted training beats general core work.
- **Supervision matters.** A 2026 RCT (60 women) found **supervised** PFMT dramatically out-performed unsupervised home training: pad-test leakage fell **22.9 g → 3.2 g** (vs essentially no change unsupervised), and 67% reached strong (Oxford 4–5) muscle grades vs 13%. If you can, get coached — at least at the start.
- **Add e-stim when muscles are very weak.** A multicentre, double-blind RCT (*EJOG*, 2026; 42 women) found adding **sEMG-triggered intravaginal electrical stimulation** to supervised PFMT produced **earlier, greater, and longer-lasting** improvements in strength and continence, sustained at 12 months — a useful boost for women who can barely activate the pelvic floor.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps.** Confirm activation with a clinician or biofeedback; supervised programs reliably outperform going it alone.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
Read "alternative" as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard HER2-targeted therapy** — not instead of it. Two themes stand out this week.

- **Correct vitamin D if you're deficient.** A 2026 retrospective interventional study (*Nutrients*; 196 early-stage HER2+ patients on trastuzumab-based therapy) found that patients who **failed** to correct a vitamin D deficiency had a **~1.7× higher recurrence hazard**, with a dose-response trend favoring higher D25 levels. The authors also note two 2025 RCTs showing a **doubling of pathologic complete response (pCR)** with vitamin D repletion, strongest in **HER2+ and triple-negative** subtypes. Signal, not proof — prospective trials are warranted.
- **Curcumin: helpful for a side effect, not a cure.** A 2026 meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (945 patients) found curcumin **reduced the severity of radiation dermatitis** (RR 0.51) but showed **no benefit** for tumor response, survival, or overall toxicity — and it **can interact** with chemotherapy, tamoxifen, and blood thinners. A 2026 *Frontiers in Oncology* review echoes the core limits: poor bioavailability and real interaction risks.
- **TP53/p53 context.** Germline **TP53** alterations (Li-Fraumeni) raise caution around radiation exposure and favor close genetic counseling — a reason to coordinate *every* integrative choice with your oncology team, since supplement-drug interactions can blunt or complicate targeted therapy.

Important framing: much of this is **early, observational, or supportive-care** evidence. Use integrative options as clinician-approved **add-ons**, never as substitutes for HER2-directed treatment.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or **fragmented** sleep, 2025–2026 guidance keeps **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements.**

- **CBT-I is first-line — and now pocket-sized.** A 2026 multi-society Australian position statement reaffirms **multicomponent CBT-I** as first-line for chronic insomnia, effective across comorbidities and delivery formats (in-person, tele-health, or self-guided digital). A 2026 RCT of **Hvil**, a 9-week fully automated **smartphone CBT-I** program (165 adults), significantly cut insomnia severity (Cohen's d 0.66) and improved **nocturnal awakenings**, sleep quality, and fatigue — good news for access.
- **Sleep hygiene alone isn't treatment.** The same guideline is blunt: generic sleep-hygiene tips are **not adequate** as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia.
- **Supplements, honestly.** The 2025 VA/DoD insomnia guideline **suggests against** melatonin, chamomile, passionflower, saffron, and valerian for chronic insomnia, and finds **insufficient evidence** to recommend for or against **magnesium**. Melatonin is best reserved for **circadian issues** (jet lag, shift work), not chronic insomnia.
- **Medications.** If drugs are needed, benzodiazepines/Z-drugs are for **short-term** use (≈2–4 weeks); **dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs)** are generally reserved for chronic insomnia.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disrupted sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and start **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
